Self-Regulatory Organizations; Texas Stock Exchange LLC; Notice of Filing, and Order Granting Accelerated Approval of, a Proposed Rule Change To Amend Rule 17.111(d) (Commodity-Based Trust Shares)

1. Purpose TXSE Rule 17.111(d) currently governs the listing and trading of Commodity-Based Trust Shares on the Exchange. Under the existing rule, the Exchange is required to submit a separate proposed rule change pursuant to Section 19(b) of the Act before listing Commodity-Based Trust Shares. The Exchange proposes to amend Rule 17.111(d) to establish generic listing standards that would permit the Exchange to list and trade Commodity-Based Trust Shares that satisfy the requirements of Rule 17.111(d) pursuant to Rule 19b-4(e) under the Act. Commodity-Based Trust Shares that do not satisfy the applicable generic listing standards could continue to be listed pursuant to a separate proposed rule change under Section 19(b) of the Act. Background The proposed standards are substantially similar to generic listing standards previously approved by the Commission for Nasdaq, Cboe BZX, and NYSE Arca. In July 2026, the Commission approved amendments to Nasdaq's generic listing standards that, among other things, permit up to 15% of the net asset value (``NAV'') of a Trust's holdings to consist of certain digital commodities and securities that do not otherwise satisfy the applicable generic eligibility criteria, add a definition of ``digital commodity,'' and permit actively managed Commodity-Based Trust Shares, subject to additional safeguards. The Commission subsequently approved substantially similar amendments for NYSE Arca and Cboe BZX and materially identical amendments for Nasdaq Texas. The Exchange's proposal incorporates both the original generic listing standards and the subsequent amendments into Rule 17.111(d), with changes necessary to conform the Exchange's existing rule structure, definitions, and cross-references. Proposal The Exchange proposes to amend Rule 17.111(d) to permit the Exchange to list and trade Commodity-Based Trust Shares that satisfy the requirements of Rule 17.111(d) pursuant to Rule 19b-4(e) under the Act. Rule 19b-4(e) provides that the listing and trading of a new derivative securities product by a self-regulatory organization is not deemed a proposed rule change pursuant to Rule 19b-4(c)(1) if the Commission has approved, pursuant to Section 19(b) of the Act, the self-regulatory organization's trading rules, procedures, and listing standards for the product class that would include the new derivative securities product and the self-regulatory organization has a surveillance program for the product class. Consistent with the Commission-approved generic listing standards, the Exchange would retain the ability to submit a proposed rule change pursuant to Section 19(b) of the Act to list and trade Commodity-Based Trust Shares that do not satisfy one or more of the applicable generic listing standards. The proposed rule would also provide that statements or representations contained in any such proposed rule change concerning (1) the description of the index, Trust holdings, or reference assets; (2) limitations on the index, Trust holdings, or reference assets; (3) the dissemination and availability of the index, Trust holdings, reference assets, or Intraday Indicative Values; or (4) the applicability of Exchange listing rules would constitute continued listing requirements. An issuer would be required to notify the Exchange of any failure to comply with such continued listing requirements. If the Commodity-Based Trust Shares do not satisfy those requirements, the Exchange may suspend trading and will initiate delisting proceedings under the TXSE Rule Series 16.500. Definitions The Exchange also proposes to modernize the definition of Commodity-Based Trust Shares in renumbered Rule 17.111(d)(3). As proposed, Commodity-Based Trust Shares could be issued by a trust, limited liability company, partnership, or other similar entity that, if applicable, is operated by a registered commodity pool operator pursuant to the Commodity Exchange Act and is not registered as an investment company under the Investment Company Act of 1940, or a series or class thereof. Consistent with its stated investment objective and policies, a Trust could hold one or more commodities or commodity-based assets and, in addition, securities, cash and cash equivalents. The proposed rule would also retain the existing creation and redemption structure, as expanded to accommodate the broader range of permitted holdings and cash creations and redemptions based on the next determined NAV per Trust share. The Exchange also proposes to amend the definition of ``commodity'' in Rule 17.111(d)(3)(B) to provide that the term is defined in Section 1a(9) of the Commodity Exchange Act and does not include an ``excluded commodity'' as defined in Section 1a(19) of the Commodity Exchange Act. Proposed Rule 17.111(d)(3)(C) would define the term ``commodity- based asset'' as any future, option, or swap on a commodity, as defined in proposed Rule 17.111(d)(3)(B). Proposed Rule 17.111(d)(3)(D) would define the term ``digital commodity'' as a commodity that is a digital asset and is intrinsically linked to and derives its value from the programmatic operation of a functional crypto system, as well as supply and demand dynamics, rather than from the expectation of profits from the essential managerial efforts of others. Proposed Rule 17.111(d)(3)(E) would define the term ``cash equivalent'' as a short-term instrument with a maturity of less than three months consisting of: (1) U.S. Government securities, including bills, notes, and bonds differing as to maturity and rates of interest, that are either issued or guaranteed by the U.S. Treasury or by U.S. Government agencies or instrumentalities; (2) certificates of deposit issued against funds deposited in a bank or savings and loan association; (3) bankers' acceptances; (4) repurchase agreements and reverse repurchase agreements; (5) bank time deposits; (6) commercial paper; and (7) money market funds. 1. Purpose When in September of this year the Exchange updated its rulebook at Equity 1 and Equity 4 to more closely align those rules with the equivalent rules of The Nasdaq Stock Market LLC (``Nasdaq''), in anticipation of the Exchange becoming a primary listing venue in 2027, the Exchange mistakenly copied an obsolete version of Nasdaq Equity 4, Rule 4120. The Commission had approved the current version of Nasdaq Equity 4, Rule 4120, back in 2022. However, this version of the rule did not become operative until August of this year. This delay in making the 2022 changes operative on Nasdaq led to the Exchange mistakenly copying in its September 2026 filing an obsolete version of Nasdaq Equity 4, Rule 4120. The Exchange proposes to correct this mistake in this filing. The Exchange proposes to replace in its entirety its current version of Equity 4, Rule 4120, with the version of that rule that is currently found in the Nasdaq rulebook. Therefore, the new version of Nasdaq Texas Equity 4, Rule 4120, would be structured as follows: 1. Section (a) (Definitions) defines certain terms that are used in the rule. 2. Section (b) (Regulatory Halts) establishes the Exchange's authority to initiate regulatory halts or pauses in various circumstances, including: halts provided for by the applicable SIP Plan; discretionary Regulatory Halts relating to issuer information, material news, initial public offerings, index warrants, derivative securities products, foreign securities, market disruptions, and Initial ETP Opens; and mandatory Regulatory Halts relating to dissemination issues for derivative securities products, the Limit Up- Limit Down Mechanism, market-wide circuit breakers, Equity Investment Tracking Stocks and Subscription Receipts, and reverse stock splits. 3. Section (c) (Operational Halts) establishes the Exchange's authority and procedures for initiating and terminating Operational Halts, including: the circumstances in which Nasdaq Texas may declare an Operational Halt, notification to the SIP when Nasdaq Texas has concerns about collecting and transmitting quotation or transaction information or has declared an Operational Halt or suspension, and the procedures for resuming trading when Nasdaq Texas determines that trading may resume in a fair and orderly manner. The changes that the Exchange would make to the Nasdaq rule to tailor it to the Exchange would be the following: 1. Modify references to the operating hours and trading sessions of the Exchange, so that they correctly reflect those of Nasdaq Texas. This includes not carrying over language in Nasdaq Equity 4, Rule 4120, that pertains to Nasdaq's upcoming transition to trading 23 hours a day, 5 days a week. 2. Eliminate references to a direct listing with capital raise, as that option is not present in the Nasdaq Texas rulebook. 3. Update references to ``Nasdaq'' with ``Nasdaq Texas.'' Additionally, the Exchange will not copy references to the CORE FIX order entry protocol that are currently present in Nasdaq Equity 4, Rule 4120. This is because the Exchange, Nasdaq, and Nasdaq PHLX LLC will be imminently submitting separate filings to abandon their plans to deploy the CORE FIX order entry protocol, due to a lack of interest by exchange participants. Therefore, it makes no sense for the Exchange to copy references to CORE FIX in Nasdaq Equity 4, Rule 4120, that will soon become obsolete. 2. Statutory Basis The Exchange believes that its proposal is consistent with Section 6(b) of the Act, in general, and furthers the objectives of Section 6(b)(5) of the Act, in particular, in that it is designed to promote just and equitable principles of trade, to remove impediments to and perfect the mechanism of a free and open market and a national market system, and, in general to protect investors and the public interest. The Exchange believes that the proposed rule change will remove impediments to, and perfect the mechanism of, a free and open market and a national market system by aligning the Exchange's rulebook at Equity 4, Rule 4120, with the substantially similar rule of Nasdaq, which was previously approved by the Commission, finding it to be consistent with the Act. The proposal is also consistent with Section 6(b)(5) because it is designed to promote clarity, consistency, and transparency for Participants, issuers, and market participants by replacing stale rule text with the version of Equity 4, Rule 4120, that reflects the Commission-approved Nasdaq framework and the intervening updates already incorporated into Nasdaq's current operative rule. In approving that framework, the Commission recognized that the revisions promote a clear and uniform approach to trading halts, improve coordination and certainty among plan participants and market participants, enhance the resiliency and integrity of market systems, and promote fair and orderly markets and investor protection. Self-Regulatory Organizations; New York Stock Exchange LLC; Notice of Filing and Immediate Effectiveness of Proposed Rule Change To Amend Exchange Rule 2(c)

1. Purpose The Exchange proposes to amend Rule 2 (``Member,'' ``Membership,'' ``Member Firm,'' etc.) to restore language inadvertently omitted from the proposed definition of ``associated person'' in a recent rule filing. More specifically, the proposed change is a technical amendment that would ensure that the persons encompassed by the ``approved person'' category that the Exchange recently filed to delete are captured by the definition of ``associated person'' in Rule 2(c) for jurisdictional and all other applicable Exchange rules. The proposed rule change is not intended to effect any substantive change to the scope of the Exchange's jurisdiction. Background and Proposed Rule Change On September 18, 2026, the Exchange filed an immediately effective rule change to (1) eliminate the ``approved person'' registration category as no longer necessary, (2) adopt a new definition of ``associated person'' in Rule 2(c) based on the definition of associated person in Rule 1011(b) of the Financial Industry Regulatory Authority, Inc. (``FINRA'') and elements of the current definition of approved person, and (3) make related technical and conforming changes. The Approved Person Filing is scheduled to become operative on October 18, 2026. As described in the Approved Person Filing, the Exchange did not intend to expand or narrow the scope of its jurisdiction. Rather, the proposal was designed to ensure that all persons currently encompassed by the approved person category would continue to be covered under the proposed definition of ``associated person.'' Specifically, the filing stated that proposed Rule 2(c)(3) would include the existing categories of approved persons: (i) persons that control a member organization; (ii) persons engaged in a securities or kindred business that is controlled by a member or member organization; and (iii) U.S. registered broker-dealers under common control with a member organization. The filing further explained that the proposed definition of ``Control Person'' was intended to encompass those same categories. The Exchange has since determined that the text of proposed Rule 2(c)(3), as filed, inadvertently omitted the clause covering persons engaged in a securities or kindred business that is controlled by a member or member organization. That clause appears in the Exchange's current approved person definition and was intended to be carried forward without substantive change. Consequently, the text of proposed Rule 2(c)(3) is inconsistent with both the description of the proposal and the Exchange's stated intent in the Approved Person Filing, which was to preserve, rather than modify, the existing scope of Exchange jurisdiction. Specifically, NSCC proposes to modify the NSCC Rules to (i) include authorized participants in the ETF reasonability check process; (ii) clarify that Index Receipt Agents and authorized participants are required to subscribe to NSCC's designated communication method for pended transaction data and identify and regularly maintain contact persons authorized to receive notifications and review and confirm the validity of pended transactions (such persons being ``authorized approvers''); and (iii) clarify requirements concerning the form, manner and timing for such confirmations. Each share of an ETF represents an undivided interest in the underlying assets of the ETF. NSCC facilitates central counterparty clearing and settlement of the creation and redemption of ETF shares in the primary market as well as clearing of ETF trades in the secondary market. The participants in the ETF primary market typically consist of the issuers of ETFs (``ETF Sponsors''), custodian banks (``ETF Agents,'' also referred to as ``Index Receipt Agents'' in the NSCC Rules), and brokers/dealers that have agreements directly with ETF Sponsors to allow the brokers/dealers to place orders for the creation and redemption of ETF shares (referred to as ``authorized participants''). Both ETF Agents and authorized participants are Members of NSCC. In general, authorized participants create and redeem ETF shares from the ETF Sponsors in blocks called ``creation units.'' An authorized participant that purchases a creation unit of ETF shares delivers a ``basket'' of securities and other assets to the ETF Agent and then receives the creation unit of ETF shares in return for those assets. The redemption process is the reverse of the creation process; the authorized participant redeems a creation unit of ETF shares in exchange for a basket of securities and other assets. Background Currently, Options 4, Section 5(d) provides that, except as otherwise provided in the Supplementary Material thereto, the interval between strike prices of series of options on individual stocks will be: (1) $2.50 or greater where the strike price is $25.00 or less; (2) $5.00 or greater where the strike price is greater than $25.00; and (3) $10.00 or greater where the strike price is greater than $200.00. Self-Regulatory Organizations: Long-Term Stock Exchange, Inc.; Notice of Filing and Immediate Effectiveness of Proposed Rule Change To Amend LTSE Rule 3.291

1. Purpose The Exchange proposes to amend LTSE Rule 3.291, Influencing or Rewarding Employees of Others; Gratuities, to conform the rule so that it is substantially similar to FINRA Rule 3220. The Exchange notes that this filing is based on a proposal recently submitted by FINRA, and approved by the Commission, to amend FINRA Rule 3220 (Influencing or Rewarding Employees of Others). Pursuant to Rule 17d-2 under the Act, the Exchange and FINRA entered into an agreement to allocate regulatory responsibility for common rules (the ``17d-2 Agreement''). The 17d-2 Agreement covers common members of the Exchange and FINRA and allocates to FINRA regulatory responsibility, with respect to common members, for the following: (i) examination of common members of the Exchange and FINRA for compliance with certain federal securities laws, rules and regulations and rules of the Exchange that the Exchange has certified as identical or substantially similar to FINRA rules; (ii) investigation of common members of the Exchange and FINRA for violations of certain federal securities laws, rules or regulations, or Exchange rules that the Exchange has certified as identical or substantially similar to a FINRA rule; and (iii) enforcement of compliance by common members with certain federal securities laws, rules and regulations, and the rules of the Exchange that the Exchange has certified as identical or substantially similar to FINRA rules. The 17d-2 Agreement included a certification by the Exchange that states that the requirements contained in certain Exchange rules are identical to, or substantially similar to, certain FINRA rules that have been identified as comparable. To conform to comparable FINRA rules for purposes of the 17d-2 Agreement, the Exchange proposes conforming the text of LTSE Rule 3.291 so that it is substantially similar to FINRA Rule 3220. Currently, LTSE Rule 3.291 is excluded from the 17d-2 Agreement because it is not identical, or substantially similar, to FINRA Rule 3220. Current LTSE Rule 3.291 prohibits a Member or person associated with a Member from directly or indirectly, giving or permitting to be given anything of value, including gratuities, in excess of one hundred dollars per individual per year to any person, principal, proprietor, employee, agent or representative of another person where such payment or gratuity is in relation to the business of the employer of the recipient of the payment or gratuity. FINRA Rule 3220 currently prohibits gifts in excess of $300.00, where the gift or gratuity is in relation to the business of the employer of the recipient. Unlike FINRA Rule 3220, current LTSE Rule 3.291 does not include provisions covering: supervision and record keeping requirements; an exclusion for payments made pursuant to bona fide, written employment contracts; gifts incidental to business entertainment; valuation of gifts; aggregation of gifts; personal gifts; bereavement gifts; de minimis gifts and promotional or commemorative items; donations due to federally declared major disasters; or gifts to a Member's associated persons or individual retail customers. LTSE Rule 3.291 was, therefore, excluded from the 17d-2 Agreement because it was not identical or substantially similar to FINRA Rule 3220. To harmonize its rules with FINRA, the Exchange proposes to conform the rule text of LTSE Rule 3.291 to text that is substantially similar to FINRA Rule 3220 so that it may be incorporated into the 17d-2 Agreement in its entirety. The Exchange believes that these changes will help to avoid confusion among Members of the Exchange that are also members of FINRA by harmonizing LTSE Rule 3.291 with FINRA Rule 3220. The proposed changes to LTSE Rule 3.291 are designed to enable the Exchange to incorporate LTSE Rule 3.291 into the 17d-2 Agreement, further reducing duplicative regulation of Members that are also members of FINRA. For the avoidance of doubt, LTSE Rule 3.291 would equally apply to Exchange-only Members as the Exchange believes it appropriately protects against improprieties, such as conflicts of interest, that might arise when a Member or person associated with a Member gives items of value to an employee of another person, such as an institutional customer, vendor or counterparty with the hope of strengthening the relationship with the customer. First, the Exchange proposes to amend LTSE Rule 3.291(a) to increase the gift limit from $100 to $300 per individual per year. FINRA stated that the current gift limit of $100 has been in place since 1992. FINRA increased the gift limit from $100 to $300 to account for past inflation since 1992 and to account for expected future inflation for approximately ten years, thereby reducing the frequency of future upward adjustments to account for inflation. Consistent with FINRA's determination, the Exchange believes that a $300 gift limit would continue to permit the exchange of business courtesies while helping to guard against excessiveness, and reasonably reflects changes to purchasing power due to inflation since the gift limit was last raised in 1992 as well as approximately ten years of expected future inflation.
